quote: It looks like it should be possible, if you do things that are advanced and recursive and have nontrivial (but consistent) structure.
content: It has proved very hard. MIRI's own later work on "corrigibility" found no satisfactory way to make a utility maximizer indifferent to being shut down without creating other perverse incentives (Soares et al., "Corrigibility," AAAI workshop, 2015; no DOI). Thornley (2024) proves theorems showing that agents meeting plausible conditions will often have incentives either to prevent shutdown or to cause it. The controlled shutdown that "looks like it should be possible" remains an open problem, hemmed in by impossibility results.

quote: And that was, effectively, the end of the Nazi atomic weapons program.
content: The essay's only historical example of an ethical injunction is a case where the injunction was broken, and the author "can't say a word against it": Haukelid let a civilian who had helped him sail to his death to protect the mission. The history also undercuts the justification. By 1942 the German leadership had judged a bomb infeasible within the war and given the project low priority, as the next sentence concedes ("Germany very likely wouldn't have gotten the Bomb anyway"). The heavy water mattered for a reactor program that was far from a weapon (Walker, German National Socialism and the Quest for Nuclear Power, 1989; book, no DOI). The one real case shows an injunction overridden for a benefit that probably didn't exist.

quote: All the happiness that the warm thought of an afterlife ever produced in humanity, has now been more than cancelled by the failure of humanity to institute systematic cryonic preservations
content: This accounting assumes that cryonics works, that bodies preserved with current methods can be revived, which no one has shown. It puts a value on the unrealized benefit without estimating its probability. That is the move "When (Not) to Use Probabilities" condemns: a confident net verdict with no numbers behind it. It also assumes, without evidence, that belief in an afterlife is why cryonics wasn't adopted.

quote: Hobbes said, “I don’t know what’s worse, the fact that everyone’s got a price, or the fact that their price is so low.”
content: There is no such line in Hobbes. The idea that "every man has his price" is attached to Robert Walpole through William Coxe's 1798 memoir ("All those men have their price"), and the "so low" addition has no traceable source. Misattributing a quotation is minor, but the sequence treats this kind of slip as a sign of unexamined belief.

quote: Self-deceptions are the worst kind of black swan bets, much worse than lies
content: The argument proves too much. Any policy can blow up for reasons outside the decider's model, honesty included. The Gestapo example two paragraphs earlier is a case where telling the truth blows up catastrophically. The argument needs evidence that self-deception carries a fatter tail of harms than the alternatives, and none is offered. The evidence that exists is mixed. Positive illusions correlate with some measures of well-being (Taylor & Brown 1988), though that reading is contested (Colvin & Block 1994). Placebos can work even when patients are told they are placebos (Kaptchuk et al. 2010), which suggests some benefits of belief are available without deception. The injunction may be wise, but the black-swan argument doesn't establish it.

quote: Always the modification is toward lenience, never to be more strict.
content: The essay refutes this a few paragraphs earlier: "I've had to make my ethics much stricter than what my parents and Jerry Pournelle and Richard Feynman told me not to do." Moral history is full of people making their ethics stricter, often against their own interests: abolitionists, vegetarians, effective altruists, the author himself. The claim that people who reason about ethics always reason toward lenience overgeneralizes from the arguments the author finds annoying.

quote: “Where there’s a will to failure, obstacles can be found.”
content: The line, unattributed here, is usually credited to John McCarthy. It is used to explain moral failure as a "will to fail," which is the correspondence bias Book II discusses: blaming other people's choices on their disposition rather than their situation. The people who "come to me and say" it is rational to do something unethical may be wrong. "They want to fail" is not a diagnosis.
